web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: The Forensic Audit: 13x Revenue Scale, Near-Zero Debt, and Working-Capital Reality
question: Does Groww's balance sheet and multi-year financial record support durable compounding, or are there hidden accounting and liquidity vulnerabilities?

epigraph.quote: Show me a financial platform with 60% operating margins and shrinking debt, and I will still check the working-capital footnotes before I trust it.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Desk

web_blocks.html: Over the five reported fiscal years from FY22 through TTM (Sep 2026), Billionbrains Garage Ventures has scaled consolidated revenue more than 13-fold, from ₹427 crore in FY22 to ₹4,645 crore in FY26 and ₹5,724 crore TTM [1]. Operating profit swung from -₹233 crore in FY22 to +₹2,744 crore in FY26 and +₹3,596 crore TTM, with operating margins expanding from -55% to 63% TTM (64.5% in Q2 FY27) [1, 3]. Excluding the one-time FY24 -₹1,337 crore reverse-flip tax distortion, core Profit Before Tax compounded from ₹504 crore in FY23 to ₹2,464 crore in FY25, ₹2,821 crore in FY26, and ₹3,657 crore TTM [1, 13].

web_blocks.title: Balance Sheet Fortress, Debt De-Leveraging & Institutional Shareholding

web_blocks.html: Groww's balance sheet as of September 2026 shows ₹19,792 crore in total assets backed by ₹11,568 crore in shareholders' equity (₹1,248 crore Equity Capital + ₹10,320 crore Reserves) [1]. Total borrowings peaked at ₹610 crore in March 2025, fell to ₹292 crore in March 2026, and declined further to just ₹77 crore by September 2026—making the platform virtually debt-free with a debt-to-equity ratio below 0.01x [1]. Fixed assets jumped from ₹402 crore (Mar 2025) to ₹1,492 crore (Mar 2026). This reflects goodwill/intangibles and infrastructure from inorganic expansion such as Fisdom, while Investments grew to ₹3,396 crore and Other Assets (including MTF receivables and client/exchange balances) reached ₹14,929 crore [1]. Meanwhile, institutional ownership has steadily deepened from Dec 2025 to Sep 2026: FIIs rose from 3.13% to 10.90% and DIIs from 4.92% to 12.73% alongside stable Promoter holding of 27.14% [1].

Cash conversion requires careful interpretation. CFO/EBITDA stood at 144% (FY22), 150% (FY23), and 157% (FY24) when pure broking float was a net cash source, before dropping to 37% in FY25 (CFO -₹962 Cr) and 26% in FY26 (CFO -₹21 Cr) as MTF lending and working-capital deployment absorbed cash [1, 20]. Importantly, Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) stands at 37.3% and Return on Equity (ROE) at 28.8% (3-year average ROE 33.9%) [1]. Working capital days remain deeply negative (-257 days in FY26) due to client/float payables. Meanwhile, debtor days ticked up modestly from 9 to 22 days as MTF and advisory receivables scaled [1].

web_blocks.title: Forensic Sign-Off: Three Balance-Sheet Guardrails
paragraphs: 1. Earnings Cleanliness: Excluding the FY24 -₹1,337 Cr reverse-flip tax distortion, core PBT has compounded cleanly from ₹504 Cr (FY23) to ₹2,464 Cr (FY25), ₹2,821 Cr (FY26), and ₹3,657 Cr TTM [1, 13].
2. Solvency Cushion: ₹11,568 Cr of net worth against ₹77 Cr of borrowings provides massive capital buffer for MTF and NBFC growth without external leverage risk [1].
3. Cash-Conversion Watch: Monitor whether CFO turns structurally positive once MTF book growth stabilizes relative to annual PAT (>₹2,693 Cr TTM) [1].

web_blocks.html: Separating accounting earnings from cash flow is the single most important forensic exercise in Groww's financial statements [22]. In FY25 and FY26, reported PAT jumped to ₹1,824 crore and ₹2,083 crore respectively, yet Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) printed negative (-₹962 crore in FY25 and -₹21 crore in FY26) [22]. On a superficial screen, negative CFO alongside record profits looks like an earnings-quality red flag. In reality, under Indian accounting standards for broking and NBFC-adjacent businesses, deploying shareholder equity and cash into the Margin Trading Facility (MTF) loan book and settlement/exchange margin receivables flows through working capital inside CFO—meaning Groww is intentionally reinvesting its cash profits into high-yielding secured client margin loans rather than suffering uncollected receivables [6][22].
Read the cash flow with care. Profits are real. Debt is tiny. Cash funds MTF growth. Equity sits near ₹11,568 crore.

book_paragraphs: When we step into the forensic vault in Chapter 6, we strip away the product demos and look strictly at the accounting trail from FY22 through September 2026.

Start with the profit-and-loss trajectory. Revenue grew from ₹427 crore in FY22 to ₹1,142 crore in FY23, ₹2,794 crore in FY24, ₹4,061 crore in FY25, ₹4,645 crore in FY26, and ₹5,724 crore on a trailing twelve-month basis through September 2026. That is more than a thirteen-fold expansion in under five years. Even more striking is what happened to operating margins: -55% in FY22, 35% in FY23, 27% in FY24, 62% in FY25, 59% in FY26, and 63% TTM. Once you strip out the one-time ₹1,337 crore reverse-flip tax hit in FY24, Groww's profit before tax marched from ₹504 crore in FY23 to ₹2,464 crore in FY25, ₹2,821 crore in FY26, and ₹3,657 crore TTM.

Now turn to the balance sheet, because this is where great fintech stories either hold together or quietly rot. As of September 2026, Groww sits on ₹19,792 crore of total assets and ₹11,568 crore of shareholders' equity (₹1,248 crore equity capital plus ₹10,320 crore of reserves). Borrowings, which briefly rose to ₹610 crore in March 2025, have been paid down to ₹292 crore in March 2026 and a negligible ₹77 crore by September 2026. That gives you a 37.3% Return on Capital Employed and a 28.8% Return on Equity on an essentially unlevered balance sheet.

Two items in the balance sheet and cash-flow statements do deserve your ongoing scrutiny. First, Fixed Assets jumped from ₹402 crore in March 2025 to ₹1,492 crore in March 2026—reflecting the accounting footprint of acquisitions like Fisdom and platform infrastructure. Second, as we diagnosed in Chapter 3, CFO/EBITDA fell from 157% in FY24 to 37% in FY25 and 26% in FY26 because scaling the MTF book to ₹4,351 crore and holding higher working-capital assets absorbed cash inside operating cash flow.

Notice also who sits on the cap table. Between December 2025 and September 2026, Promoter holding remained steady at 27.14%, while FIIs climbed from 3.13% to 10.90% and DIIs rose from 4.92% to 12.73%. Put all six chapters together, and the business-quality verdict is clear: Groww is a structurally advantaged, high-margin, #1 market-share platform actively diversifying away from F&O—not yet immune to SEBI or market cycles, which is why we keep a close watch on derivatives concentration and MTF cash conversion, but undeniably a high-quality franchise.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A 37.3% ROCE, 28.8% ROE, and ₹77 crore of debt against ₹11,568 crore of equity means Groww's balance sheet can survive a severe regulatory or market winter. The only open forensic test is watching CFO normalize as MTF growth matures.

book_subsections.title: Forensic Deep-Dive: Reconciling Record Profits with Negative Operating Cash Flow
paragraphs: If there is one chapter where lazy investors get tripped up on Groww, it is Chapter 6. Pull up Groww's five-year cash flow statement and you will notice an apparent paradox: in FY24, net profit was negative ₹805 crore while operating cash flow was positive ₹885 crore; in FY25 and FY26, net profit exploded to ₹1,824 crore and ₹2,083 crore, yet operating cash flow turned negative at -₹962 crore and -₹21 crore.

Let us decode both halves of that paradox cleanly. FY24's accounting loss was purely the non-recurring ₹1,339.7 crore tax on flipping the parent company from Delaware to India—while core operations were already cash-generative. Conversely, FY25 and FY26's negative CFO happened because Groww grew its MTF lending book and exchange settlement receivables by thousands of crores. In accounting, lending money to margin-trading clients is booked as a working-capital outflow inside operating cash flow, even though it creates a high-yielding, share-collateralized asset on the balance sheet. Meanwhile, borrowings stand at a negligible ₹77 crore against ₹11,568 crore of shareholders' equity as of September 2026—a fortress balance sheet by any standard.

book_subsections.title: Balance Sheet Fortress: Equity Cushion vs. Working Capital Needs
paragraphs: As of September 2026, Groww sits on ₹11,568 crore of shareholders' equity (₹1,248 crore equity capital plus ₹10,320 crore reserves) against just ₹77 crore of borrowings—essentially zero financial leverage. Total assets stand at ₹19,792 crore, including ₹3,396 crore of investments and ₹14,929 crore of other assets largely representing client/exchange settlement balances and MTF receivables.

Why does this fortress equity base matter? Because scaling an MTF book from ₹4,351 crore toward ₹8,000 crore requires capital. Brokers with thin balance sheets must borrow expensive short-term debt or dilute shareholders via equity raises to fund client margin lending. Groww can fund its next ₹3,000–₹4,000 crore of MTF expansion entirely out of retained internal accruals—earning ~14%–15% gross yield on shareholder equity without taking on corporate debt risk.

book_subsections.title: Tax Rate, Other Income, and Clean Earnings Quality Post-IPO
paragraphs: Checking the tax and other-income lines confirms that Groww's recent profitability is clean and repeatable. Effective tax rates in FY25 and FY26 settled consistently at 26 percent—right in line with India's statutory corporate tax regime—and Q1 and Q2 FY27 both printed 26 percent tax rates. Other income contributed ₹171 crore in FY26 (just 3.7 percent of revenue), primarily treasury yields on corporate cash rather than one-off asset sales. That means the 62 to 64 percent operating margins and ₹2,693 crore TTM net profit reflect genuine core operating economics.
